---
name: project-setup
description: 'Sets up Toolkit V2 in a new project, or checks, updates, and repairs an existing setup, including Notion and Hindsight. Use when the owner says "set up Toolkit V2", "set up this project", "check the setup", or "update the toolkit", or starts working on a new computer.'
---

# Project setup

Voice: write to the owner in plain English. Claude Code: follow the project's Plain English output style. Codex: follow the "How to write replies" section of `AGENTS.md`.
The interview wording and what setup installs: `references/interview.md`. Repair, switching, new computer, and wiring: `references/repair-and-wiring.md`. Run each `toolkit` command alone, on its own line, in both hosts: never joined by `&&`, `;`, or a pipe, and never from a script (in Codex that runs it inside the sandbox, which blocks Notion, Hindsight, and `.codex/`). Text: one-line values (`--name`, `--owner`) go in single quotes, with an apostrophe written `'\''`, because double quotes run backticks and `$(...)`; the current focus goes on standard input in Claude Code (`<file>` is `-`, followed by a quoted heredoc, `<<'EOF'`) and in `--text '<text>'` in Codex, never through a file at a fixed name such as `/tmp/focus.md`. Ask the owner in the reply text, one question per message, never through a question tool.

## Steps

1. Check the setup. If `toolkit` is not found, run `node <this skill's folder>/../../bin/toolkit machine-setup` (the skill's folder is the one holding this file). If doctor reports a computer problem, run machine-setup. machine-setup also changes `~/.codex/config.toml`: it turns off, for every Codex folder, each Toolkit V2 plugin that `codex plugin add` turned on there (projects turn them on for themselves); say that in one line and get the owner's yes before the first run on a computer. Name anything the owner must do himself: `ntn login` opens a browser sign-in; trusting the hooks in Codex happens in its `/hooks` screen. Never do those for him. This skill sets up Toolkit V2, never the older claude-toolkit (its `project-init` skill); when the owner names Toolkit V2 and only `project-init` is listed, say so and use this skill's steps. A new computer, or a toolkit update, also needs the plugins installed or updated in each host, Codex included: in Codex, `codex plugin marketplace add`, then `codex plugin add` for each of the six plugins, then machine-setup (`references/repair-and-wiring.md`, "A new computer" and "Updating the toolkit").
   `toolkit doctor`
   `toolkit machine-setup`
2. No `.toolkit.json`: a new project. Look before asking: an empty or existing repository; `sfdx-project.json` answers the Salesforce question in advance. Then ask one question at a time, each with a recommendation, in this order: the project name (with its key, id prefix, and owner name, confirmed in one line); the tracker (local folders, Notion, GitHub Issues, Jira); the memory (built-in `.memory/`, local Hindsight, Notion); Salesforce or not, and for Salesforce the sandbox and production org aliases; whether he wants `SOUL.md` (a no becomes `--decline SOUL.md`, so no later sync brings it back).
3. Run init with the answers (the second line, with `--salesforce`, for a Salesforce project; add `--decline SOUL.md` after a no). Setup copies the model scaffold and applies your answers: it copies the model project's folders and files, keeps only the blocks of `AGENTS.md`, `README.md`, and `PROJECT.md` that match the answers, fills the project name, writes the rules list and `.toolkit.json`, installs the tracker, memory, and Salesforce parts only when chosen, never copies work items or memory records, and turns the V2 plugins on and every `*@claude-toolkit` plugin off in this project. Then record the choices init has no flag for: the id prefix when it is not `WI`, and the Salesforce org aliases. With Notion, init may take another id prefix when `WI` is already used there: say the prefix it reports in one line. In Codex: init writes `.codex/` and `.agents/`, which the Codex sandbox refuses, and it writes them first. Before running it, tell the owner that Codex will ask to run it outside the sandbox. If it stops with "Could not write ... .codex/" (or `.agents/`), or says the Codex sandbox blocked its request to Hindsight, nothing else was written: stop, show him the exact command init printed, and ask him to approve it or to run it in a terminal. Never change a setup answer (hosts, tracker, memory, Salesforce) to get past an error, and never set it up in another folder and copy it over.
   `toolkit init --name '<name>' --key <key> --tracker <tracker> --memory <memory> --owner '<owner>'`
   `toolkit init --name '<name>' --key <key> --tracker <tracker> --memory <memory> --owner '<owner>' --salesforce`
   `toolkit config set tracker.idPrefix <prefix>`
   `toolkit config set salesforce.orgs.sandbox <alias>`
   `toolkit config set salesforce.orgs.production <alias>`
4. Wire the choices. Notion: check the sign-in with `ntn whoami` (if it fails, the owner runs `ntn login` himself), then build the project's pages. Hindsight: check the service (install or start it only after a yes), then create the project's bank. GitHub or Jira: show the written instructions and create nothing in that service without a yes. Salesforce: fill the API version, which the model leaves as `XX.0`. Read it from the sandbox org (the `apiVersion` field of the read-only `sf org display -o <sandbox alias> --json`), or ask the owner. Put it in `sfdx-project.json` (`sourceApiVersion`) and in the `<version>` line of `delivery/deployment/full-project-deployment-template/package.xml`; the work item templates get it when `sf-component-tracker` copies them.
   `toolkit notion ensure-root`
   `toolkit notion ensure-project --project-name '<name>'`
   `toolkit hindsight service status`
   `toolkit hindsight ensure-bank`
5. Fill the setup guides: the copied files carry fill-in guide comments and `<angle bracket>` prompts. Fill them only with facts the owner confirmed. The project's one-sentence outcome is his to say: ask for it in its own question, with a suggestion drawn from the repository, and never write it from the code, the tests, or the README; until he answers, leave the outcome prompts in `AGENTS.md`, `PROJECT.md`, and `PROJECT-ROADMAP.md` and list them. Then fill the "Build, test, or deploy" row in `AGENTS.md`, then `PROJECT.md` and `README.md` (`PROJECT-ROADMAP.md` and `requirements/SYSTEM-DATA-MODEL.md` when the facts are known), fill `SOUL.md` with his words when he wanted it, and delete each guide once its file is filled. List any prompt left for a fact nobody knows yet, including those in `PROJECT-ROADMAP.md` and `requirements/SYSTEM-DATA-MODEL.md`. A `SOUL.md` the owner turns down after init: record the no with the command below, then delete the file, so sync and doctor leave it out.
   `toolkit config set declined SOUL.md`
6. `.toolkit.json` present: repair. Show one numbered table from doctor and the dry run: missing, out of date, changed by the owner, broken wiring, each with its fix. Run sync only after a yes; it adds every missing file at once and never overwrites a file the project changed. Report a changed file as "project ahead of the toolkit".
   `toolkit sync --dry-run`
   `toolkit sync`
7. Switching memory (export, change the choice, sync, wire the new backend as in step 4, a dry-run import, then the import) or the tracker (no command yet: a preview, then moves only with the owner's yes): follow `references/repair-and-wiring.md`, "Switching the memory backend" and "Switching the tracker".
8. Run doctor until it reports 0 problems. Warnings about the other host (for example Codex hook trust, seen from Claude Code) are expected: they are the owner's steps, do not block setup, and do not make doctor fail when run from Claude Code. Setup is not a work item: create none for setup steps. An owner step that doctor checks (trust the hooks in Codex, `ntn login`) goes in the reply and in the current focus under "Waiting on the owner", marked "setup step; drop it when doctor stops reporting it"; "Start a new session" goes in the reply only. Save the focus as the header says (the first save command below in Claude Code, with the text in a quoted heredoc; the second in Codex), with the `# Current focus` title and the "Last updated" line. Then show the first briefing and explain in plain words what was set up, what was skipped, what the owner must do himself, and the prompts left. The setup files are not committed yet, and the first merge of a work item needs them committed, so the reply's last line is the offer: "Setup files are not committed. Commit them now?" Commit only after a yes, staged by name (never `git add -A`), with a plain message and no AI credit (no `Co-Authored-By` line naming an AI, no "Generated with" line); in Codex, with escalated permissions (`sandbox_permissions` set to `require_escalated`) and a one-line reason, or by the owner in a terminal when Codex refuses it without asking. After the commit, the reply's last line is "Tell me the first thing you want built."
   `toolkit memory focus --json`
   `toolkit memory focus --set-file - --expect <version>`
   `toolkit memory focus --text '<text>' --expect <version>`
   `toolkit brief`

## Steps only the owner can do

Say each one plainly, with why, and wait. Never do them for him.

- **`ntn login`**: signs the Notion command-line tool into his Notion account. It opens a browser sign-in. Needed only for a Notion tracker or Notion memory, and only when `ntn whoami` fails.
- **Trust the hooks in Codex**: open Codex in this project, type `/hooks`, and trust the Toolkit V2 hooks. Codex skips plugin hooks until he does. Needed again after the hooks change or the project folder moves.
- **Start a new session** after setup, so Claude Code loads the new settings and the Plain English style.
- **Approve Codex running the init command outside its sandbox**, when setup runs inside Codex, or run the command init printed in a terminal.
- **Start a new project from Codex:** Codex lists the Toolkit V2 skills only in a project that `toolkit init` has set up, because the V2 plugins are on only where a project's `.codex/config.toml` turns them on. In a new folder, run `toolkit init` in a terminal first (or set the project up from Claude Code), then open Codex there and say "finish setting up Toolkit V2".

## Rules

- One question per message. Every question carries a recommendation and its main reason.
- Setup is not a work item. Never create one for setup steps, and never add made-up owner questions to finish setup. Owner steps go in the final reply; the ones doctor checks also go in the current focus under "Waiting on the owner" until doctor stops reporting them.
- Never fill a fact the owner has not confirmed, above all the project's outcome. Leave the prompt and ask.
- Every step is safe to run again. When a step fails, fix the cause and run it again; init writes `.toolkit.json` last, and a second run records the files an earlier run wrote.
- Never change an answer the owner gave (tracker, memory, hosts, Salesforce, `SOUL.md`) to get past a failed command. Stop, say what failed, and say what he must approve or run.
- Nothing is created outside this project without a yes: no GitHub repository, no Jira fields, no paid service, no Notion pages outside the "AI Agent Second Brain" page.
- Instruction files follow the model: `AGENTS.md` holds the instructions, and one root `CLAUDE.md` (installed when Claude Code is a host) holds only the line `@AGENTS.md`, so Claude Code reads `AGENTS.md` through it. Doctor checks this. There is no other `CLAUDE.md`, `.claude/CLAUDE.md`, or `CLAUDE.local.md`. Because the root `CLAUDE.md` exists, Claude Code does not load a subfolder's `AGENTS.md` by itself; the root `AGENTS.md` tells the agent to read it before editing in that folder. Ask before changing or removing a `CLAUDE.md` the owner wrote.

# tally

A tiny Node.js command-line tool that counts things in text files.
## main
/Users/michaelrihm/.local/bin/toolkit

# The setup interview

Detail for `project-setup` step 2. Ask one question per message. Each
question carries a recommendation and its main reason, so the owner can
answer "yes" and move on.

## Look before asking

Check these first, without asking:

- Is this folder a Git repository? (`git rev-parse --show-toplevel`.) No
  repository: say so and offer `git init`. Toolkit V2 finds the project, the
  tracker, and memory through Git.
- Is the repository empty, or does it already hold code? Name the language
  and framework you see.
- `sfdx-project.json` present: this is a Salesforce project. Confirm it in
  one line instead of asking.
- `.toolkit.json` present with `"toolkit": "toolkit-v2"`: this is a repair,
  not a new setup (see `repair-and-wiring.md`).
- Files from an older toolkit setup (for example a `knowledge/` folder, or a
  `CLAUDE.md` with more than the line `@AGENTS.md`): tell the owner what you
  found. Toolkit V2 adds its own
  files and turns the current toolkit's plugins off for this project; it does
  not move or delete the old files. Ask before touching them. A file the
  project already has is kept, never overwritten.
- The owner name: `git config user.name`.
- `ntn whoami` (only matters for Notion): signed in or not.
- `toolkit hindsight health` (only matters for Hindsight): the local server is
  up or not.

## Question 1: the project name

Confirm the name, key, id prefix, and owner in one line:

> I'll call this project "Acme CRM" (short key `acme-crm`, work item ids `WI-001`, `WI-002`, owner Mike). Is that right?

- The key is the name in lowercase words joined by hyphens. It names the
  Hindsight memory bank and appears in the Notion page title.
- The id prefix is `WI` unless the owner wants another (for example `ACME`).
  A different prefix is set right after init, before any item exists, with
  `toolkit config set tracker.idPrefix <prefix>`.

## Question 2: where work is tracked

> Where should work items live? I recommend local folders on this computer: they are the fastest, work offline, and need nothing else set up. Choose Notion if you want to see and change the board on your phone or the web. GitHub Issues and Jira are possible, but the toolkit only gives written instructions for them.

| Choice | `--tracker` | Good when | What to know |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Local folders | `local` | A solo project on one computer | Items live in `.work-items/`, which Git ignores. They stay on this computer; `toolkit export` is the backup. |
| Notion | `notion` | The owner wants the board on his phone or the web | Needs `ntn` signed in. Each project gets its own Work Items database under the "AI Agent Second Brain" page. |
| GitHub Issues | `github` | The code and the team already live in GitHub | No driver: agents follow written instructions with `gh`. Labels are created once, with a yes. |
| Jira | `jira` | A client requires Jira | No driver: agents follow written instructions with the Jira tool the owner connects. |

## Question 3: where memory lives

> Where should the project's memory live? I recommend the built-in `.memory/` folder: it is private, fast, and needs no server. [When the tracker is Notion: I recommend Notion, so work and memory sit together and you can read both on your phone.] Hindsight is also installed on this Mac; choose it if you want search by meaning across many memories.

| Choice | `--memory` | Good when | What to know |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Built-in `.memory/` | `builtin` | Most projects | Files in the main checkout, Git-ignored, on this computer only; the `memory-tidy` skill backs it up to a folder the owner picks. |
| Local Hindsight | `hindsight` | Many memories, and search by meaning matters | The local server at `127.0.0.1:8888` must be running (a background service on this Mac). One memory bank per project. Never Hindsight Cloud. |
| Notion | `notion` | The tracker is Notion, or the owner reads memory on his phone | The project's Memory page in Notion, in the layout of Lore (Notion's open-source AI memory): the records are rows of its Memories database. Needs `ntn` signed in. |

Recommendation rule: Notion when the tracker is Notion; otherwise built-in.

## Question 4: Salesforce

Skip the yes-or-no question when `sfdx-project.json` answered it; confirm in
one line instead.

> Is this a Salesforce project? I recommend no, because I found no `sfdx-project.json`. A yes adds the Salesforce rules, the deploy and data-change skills, the protected-org guards, and the `delivery/` folder.

For a Salesforce project, ask for the org aliases, one question at a time.
Show the aliases on this computer first (`sf org list`, a read-only command):

> Which org alias is the sandbox the agents may deploy to for testing? I see `acme-uat` and `acme-dev`; I recommend `acme-uat`.

> Which org alias is production? Agents never deploy there or change its data; the guards block it and hand you the command instead. I see `acme-prod`.

Record them after init:

```text
toolkit config set salesforce.orgs.sandbox <alias>
toolkit config set salesforce.orgs.production <alias>
```

## After the answers

Say what will happen in three or four lines, then run it:

> I'll now copy the model scaffold and apply your answers: the project's folders and files from the model project, AGENTS.md with only the parts for your choices, the rules, and the settings; turn on the Toolkit V2 plugins for this project only (and turn the older toolkit's plugins off here); set up local folders for work and built-in memory. Nothing outside this folder changes.

Then `toolkit init`, the `toolkit config set` lines the answers need, the
wiring in `repair-and-wiring.md`, filling the setup guides (below), and
`toolkit doctor`.

## What setup installs

The toolkit plugin carries an exact copy of the model project in its
`scaffold/model/` folder. Setup copies that model and applies the answers:

| Installed | When |
| --- | --- |
| `AGENTS.md`, `PROJECT.md`, `PROJECT-ROADMAP.md`, `DECISIONS.md`, `README.md`, `.gitignore` | Every project |
| `SOUL.md` | Every project, unless the owner declines it (`--decline SOUL.md`, or `toolkit config set declined SOUL.md` later) |
| `requirements/` (its own `AGENTS.md`, `SYSTEM-DATA-MODEL.md`, and `system-area-template/`), `system-guide/AREA-TEMPLATE.md`, `tests/TEST-PLAN-TEMPLATE.md`, `ai-external-knowledge/INDEX.md` | Every project |
| The general rules in `.claude/rules/` | Every project (Codex reads them through `AGENTS.md`) |
| A root `CLAUDE.md` holding only `@AGENTS.md`, `.claude/settings.json`, `.claude/output-styles/plain-english.md` | Claude Code is one of the hosts |
| `.codex/config.toml` and `.codex/rules/toolkit.rules` (written by the toolkit; the model has neither) | Codex is one of the hosts |
| `.work-items/work-item-template/` (`WORK-ITEM.md`, `DESIGN.md`) and `.claude/rules/work-item-folders.md` | Local folders tracker |
| `.memory/` seed files: `AGENTS.md`, `CURRENT_FOCUS.md`, `MEMORY.md`, `memory-criteria.md`, `project_topic_template.md`, `terminology-glossary.md` | Built-in memory |
| `delivery/`, `sfdx-project.json`, `.forceignore`, `tools/kb/`, `tools/permissions/`, the two guard hooks in `.claude/hooks/`, `.claude/protected-orgs.json`, and the nine Salesforce rules | Salesforce projects |
| The `sf-*` skills in `.claude/skills/` | Salesforce projects with Claude Code as a host |
| `.codex/hooks.json` (runs the two guard hooks in Codex) and the `sf-*` skills in `.agents/skills/` | Salesforce projects with Codex as a host |

- `AGENTS.md`, `README.md`, and `PROJECT.md` carry setup markers such as
  `<!-- if tracker=local -->` ... `<!-- endif -->`. Setup keeps the lines for
  the answers given and removes the rest, markers included.
- The rules list in `AGENTS.md`, between `<!-- toolkit:rules:start -->` and
  `<!-- toolkit:rules:end -->`, is written from the files in `.claude/rules/`
  and rebuilt on every `toolkit sync`. Never edit it by hand.
- In a project that is not a Salesforce project, the Salesforce hooks and
  `sf` permission lines are left out of `.claude/settings.json`, and the
  Salesforce lines are left out of `.gitignore`.
- `.memory/MEMORY.md` is generated: setup installs the model's copy, then
  `toolkit memory reindex` rebuilds it.
- Setup never copies work items or memory records, and never copies the
  model's `.vscode/` or `.sfdx/` folders.
- `.toolkit.json` records the answers. It is written last.

## Filling the setup guides

The copied files start with a fill-in guide comment and hold `<angle bracket>`
prompts. Setup fills the project name. The rest is the agent's, with facts the
owner confirmed:

- `AGENTS.md`: the one-sentence outcome, and the "Build, test, or deploy" row
  under Commands. Ask for both, one question at a time, with a
  recommendation from what the repository shows. The outcome is the owner's
  answer, never a sentence worked out from the code, the tests, or the
  README: ask "What should this project do for you, in one sentence? From the
  code I'd suggest: <suggestion>." Until he answers, leave the outcome prompts
  in `AGENTS.md`, `PROJECT.md`, and `PROJECT-ROADMAP.md` and list them in the
  report.
- `PROJECT.md` and `README.md`: follow each file's guide. Ask only what the
  repository cannot answer.
- `PROJECT-ROADMAP.md` (the project outcome, phases, and work units) and
  `requirements/SYSTEM-DATA-MODEL.md` (accepted data model requirements):
  fill them when the owner already knows the facts. On a new project they
  usually stay as they are, and are listed in the final report as prompts
  left. The data model gets only accepted requirements, never a guess.
- `SOUL.md`: ask whether the owner wants it ("Do you want a SOUL.md that tells
  the agent how you like to work? I recommend skipping it for now; you can add
  it later."). Ask it with the other setup questions, so a no goes to init as
  `--decline SOUL.md` and the file is never installed. With a yes, fill it with
  his words and get his approval. A no after init: run
  `toolkit config set declined SOUL.md`, then delete the file. The no is kept
  in `.toolkit.json`, so sync never brings the file back and doctor does not
  report it missing. `toolkit config set declined none` undoes it.
- Delete each fill-in guide once its file is filled. Never invent a fact to
  fill a prompt: list each prompt that is left, with the fact it needs, in the
  final report.

## Explaining the result

End with a short plain report:

- What was set up, as a short list the owner can check: tracker, memory,
  Salesforce or not, the files added.
- What was skipped and why.
- What the owner must do himself (see the SKILL.md list), each with why.
  "Start a new session" goes here only. A step doctor checks (Codex hook
  trust, `ntn login`) also goes in the current focus under "Waiting on the
  owner", marked as a setup step to drop when doctor stops reporting it.
- Doctor's result: 0 problems, or each remaining problem with its fix.
  Warnings about the other host (Codex hook trust seen from Claude Code) are
  expected and are the owner's steps.
- The prompts left, each with the fact it needs.
- The last line: the commit offer ("Setup files are not committed. Commit them
  now?"), and after the commit, "Tell me the first thing you want built."

<!-- Project setup fill-in guide: toolkit init replaces <Project name>, keeps only the blocks for the tracker, memory system, and Salesforce choice made at setup, and writes the rules list. Then replace the one-sentence outcome below and the "Build, test, or deploy" row under Commands with this project's confirmed values. Change paths only when the installed folder differs. Remove this guide and every angle-bracket prompt before handing the guide to a new project agent. -->

<One sentence describing this project and its outcome.> The owner named in `PROJECT.md` makes this project's decisions. The agent runs the project: it keeps the work tracker, memory, and project records current, and it does the technical work.

## Every session

- The session-start hook adds a "Project briefing" to your context: this worktree's work item, active items with the skill that continues each one, what waits on the owner, the current focus, moved items, and setup warnings. If there is no briefing, run `toolkit brief` and read it.
- Read `SOUL.md` (when the project has one) and `PROJECT.md`; read them again after resume, clear, or compaction.
- Anything to build, add, fix, or change, and "keep going": the `work-on` skill. It opens the work item; also read the item's phase in `PROJECT-ROADMAP.md`.
- A change to a requirement, such as R-01, at any stage: `work-requirements`.
- "You drive", "take it from here", "run with it", even about a named item: `work-delegate`.
- "Where are we": `work-status`. "What do you need from me" and approvals: `work-decide`.
- "Remember", "from now on", "forget that": `memory-save`. "What did we decide": `memory-find`.
- Open the matching skill or rule when the task needs its procedure. Method skills from other plugins (brainstorming, plans, debugging) may run inside these skills, never instead of them.
- Before editing files in a folder that has its own `AGENTS.md` (for example `requirements/`), read that file.
- Codex: at session start, read the always-on rules listed under "Rules".

## What the owner decides

Ask the owner and record the answer before you:
- approve requirements (build and data-load work cannot pass stage `03` without it; requirements count as approved only when the item records the owner's approval with a date; a saved draft is not approved);
- choose or approve a design, approve a finished result, or mark work Done or Cancelled;
- merge to the default branch (unless `DECISIONS.md` records a standing merge instruction), deploy, or do anything that cannot be undone;
- spend money, sign in, or change an account.

Do everything else yourself, record it, and report it. When you need a decision, add it to the work item's Open Questions with "Decision needed from: owner" and set the item's `waiting_on` to `owner` ("Work tracking" says how).

- Tracker: local folders in `.work-items/`, Git-ignored, in the main checkout, shared by every worktree. `.claude/rules/work-item-folders.md` covers folders, moves, and generated files. A sub-item is an item folder nested inside its parent item's folder. It is the only tracker; never copy items into a second tracker or a local list.
- IDs look like `WI-001` (the prefix is `tracker.idPrefix` in `.toolkit.json`). Refer to work items by ID, never by folder path. The owner may move or rename item folders; find them by ID and continue. Change `waiting_on`, the stage, and other fields with `toolkit work` commands.
- Keep each design with its item after delivery. The roadmap names items by ID; item detail stays in the tracker.

- System: built-in memory in `.memory/`, Git-ignored, in the main checkout, shared by every worktree. It can be opened as an Obsidian vault. Read `.memory/AGENTS.md` before working there. What is worth saving: `.memory/memory-criteria.md`.
- Read and write memory only through the `memory-save`, `memory-find`, and `memory-tidy` skills, which run `toolkit memory` commands. Search memory before asking the owner to repeat something. When a save needs the owner's yes: the `memory-save` skill. Never store secrets, email addresses, or work-item status.

## How to write replies

Claude Code applies the Plain English output style to chat. Codex and helper agents follow these lines instead.

- Start with the answer, result, or current status. Answer what was asked. Keep it short; add detail when asked.
- Use ordinary words. Explain an unfamiliar term the first time it matters. Use the exact name a system uses, the same way every time.
- Write literally: no metaphors, idioms, jokes, or picture words in place of the real name. State the point directly, without a "not this, but that" setup.
- Use paragraphs for a connected explanation, bullets for separate items or choices, and a heading only when it names what is under it.
- When asking for a decision, name the choice and the difference that matters, and recommend one.
- Use the exact status word: written, built, tested, merged, installed, or seen working. Say something works only when you saw it work.
- Leave out routine narration of process and helper activity. Give one direct line when the owner lost something, an action cannot be undone, work waits on the owner, or there is a cost.

# Publish Project Documents

- In a copied Git repository, prepare each authorized documentation-only save in its own temporary Git worktree. Publish its commit directly to the default branch without a pull request.
- Rules, skills, hooks, prompts, settings, and code use a worktree and a pull request, even when written in Markdown.
- Saving a document does not approve its requirements or its build.
- Stage only this save's files, by name, in its worktree. Read the full staged diff.
- Never force-push or change another session's checkout. Resolve a remote advance in this save's worktree.
- An unpushed commit is unfinished. Verify the complete save reached the remote. In a repository with no remote (`git remote` prints nothing), the save is finished when its commit is on the local default branch.
- Steps, checks, and recovery: the `publish-docs` skill.

- `.memory/` and `.work-items/` are local and Git-ignored. Their saves do not use this publication route.
README.md

# Local project memory

Keep future sessions oriented without turning every conversation into lasting memory. This folder is the project's built-in memory store and can be opened directly as an Obsidian vault. Active topics stay flat; filenames and YAML types agree. Git ignores this folder, so back it up with `toolkit memory export --to <folder outside this project>`.

## Read and route

- Read `CURRENT_FOCUS.md` at startup; the session briefing includes it. Read `MEMORY.md` as a short index, then open relevant topics. Check dates, scope, and the current source before acting on a remembered claim.
- Read `memory-criteria.md` before selecting or changing memory. It holds the default eligibility rules; the `memory-save` skill holds the approval policy and the onboarding or trusted mode. Use the terminology glossary for project language, including distinct meanings across systems.
- Link related notes inside this vault with relative Markdown links, such as `[account model](project_account_model.md)`. Obsidian shows backlinks to a note from the notes that link to it; a second reverse link is optional. Link only when the relationship helps retrieval, and check that the target exists. Keep tracker URLs and paths outside `.memory/` as source references rather than vault links.
- Keep current tasks and owner-mentioned to-dos in `CURRENT_FOCUS.md`, naming work items by ID. Keep full tasks, status, requirements, history, and the work item's design together in the chosen tracker; verified system behavior in the System Guide; procedures in instructions or skills; and raw outside sources in their source folders.

## Curate

- Use a coherent topic file such as `project_account_data_model.md`. Allowed prefixes and matching `metadata.type` values are `user`, `feedback`, `project`, `reference`, and `event`. `project_topic_template.md` is a seed, not a saved memory. Keep one related topic per file and aim for a quick read.
- Record source and date, status, scope, the durable point, why it matters, and how to apply it. Keep uncertainty explicit. Preserve extra YAML fields written by a host or imported record.
- Search for an existing topic before creating one (`toolkit memory find`). Correct, merge, or supersede in place where possible. Mark obsolete claims in both file text and index; do not leave an archived item reading as currently open.
- When renaming, merging, archiving, or deleting a topic, inspect links from other memory notes and repair any affected links, saving each repaired note with `toolkit memory save`. Do not leave a link pointing at a former active location.
- `toolkit memory save`, `retire`, and `restore` rebuild `MEMORY.md`; run `toolkit memory reindex` after any other topic change. The index holds one short link per active topic, not the content itself. Keep it below the configured budget.
- Keep `CURRENT_FOCUS.md` under 50 lines by replacing stale sections, not appending, and write it with `toolkit memory focus --set-file`. Do not remove an unresolved owner to-do solely to meet that limit.
- Keep the glossary broad through sourced real terms, aliases, and system-specific meanings, and write it with `toolkit memory glossary --set-file`. Do not invent definitions.

## Authority and completion

- Save through the `memory-save` skill, which holds the approval policy for onboarding and trusted mode. An explicit request to remember or correct is authorization for that specific change.
- Ask before ambiguous, bulk, or irreversible deletion of unique content. Only the owner can change the mode.
- A rejected candidate is not saved to another memory, a criteria example, the glossary, or a pending queue. Record only the general selection lesson, as a `feedback` memory, if the owner gave one.
- The main agent writes this folder only with `toolkit memory` commands, for example `save`, `retire`, `focus`, `glossary`, and `reindex` (`toolkit memory --help` lists them all). They lock the folder, refuse stale edits, and rebuild the index. Never run parallel writers against the same topic.
- Read back changes with `toolkit memory get` and run `toolkit doctor` before reporting success. Memory work does not edit requirements, work-item status, designs, deployments, or source code.
